conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Dr. Carter and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m glad you’re here. Today I’d like to do a quick check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a 10-question tool that helps us see how mood and anxiety have been feeling for you over the past week. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything we discuss stays between us unless safety is a concern. We’ll just have a relaxed chat—one question at a time—so you can share as openly as you feel comfortable.

Ready to start? Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Honestly? Not very often. I’ll smile if someone makes a joke, but it feels forced—like I’m just going through the motions. Most of the time I’m too tired or worried to find anything genuinely funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I haven’t really… I can’t remember the last time I actually laughed. Even when my partner tries to be funny, it just feels flat. I’ll give a little smile so he doesn’t worry, but inside I feel kind of numb.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much lately. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now it all feels like another chore. I still go, because I know I should, but I’m not really looking forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

All the time. If the baby spits up more than usual, I assume it’s because I ate the “wrong” thing. When he wouldn’t settle last night, I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not comforting him right or I missed some cue. My head tells me babies just cry, but I still feel like I’m failing him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart starts racing—what if he chokes, what if I’m not making enough milk, what if he stops breathing in his sleep? Nothing’s actually wrong, but I can’t shake the dread. I check his breathing three, four times a night, even when he’s peacefully asleep.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a couple of times this week. Once I was just folding laundry while the baby napped and suddenly felt like I couldn’t breathe—my chest got tight, heart pounding, like something awful was about to happen. I had to sit on the floor and grip the carpet to remind myself I was still in my living room. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. Even little stuff—like when the bottles aren’t clean or I can’t find a clean onesie—feels huge. I’ll stand in the kitchen and just stare at the mess, tears welling up, thinking I’ll never get through it. I usually manage to push through, but it’s like I’m constantly treading water and my legs are exhausted.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off. I keep replaying everything I might’ve done wrong that day—did I burp him long enough, was that rash normal, am I a terrible mom? By the time I drift off the baby’s usually ready to wake up again, so I rarely get more than a couple hours in a row.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be holding the baby and suddenly feel like crying for no real reason—just this deep sadness that sits in my chest. I try to remind myself how lucky I am to have him, but the feeling doesn’t go away.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried three times since last weekend. Yesterday it was because I spilled a little pumped milk on the counter—just stood there sobbing like it was the worst thing in the world. I know it sounds silly, but in the moment it felt like proof I can’t handle anything right now.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. No matter how low I feel, I would never want to leave my baby or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he deserves.

You've shared that the last week has felt heavy and overwhelming-laughter and enjoyment seem distant, while worries about your baby's safety race through your mind day and night. Despite your deep love for him, a persistent sadness and sense of inadequacy follow you, and even small tasks feel like waves you must struggle to stay above.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly states inability to laugh or find humor, matching 'Not at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports marked reduction in anticipatory enjoyment, still participates but without pleasure—aligns with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame 'all the time' with specific examples, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Response describes near-daily intrusive worries about infant safety without real cause, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>The patient describes two clear panic-like episodes this week with physical symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart) and fear of impending doom, matching "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping with daily tasks, matching "sometimes haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent nightly difficulty sleeping due to distressing thoughts, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "pretty much every day" and describes persistent, overwhelming feelings that align with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple recent crying episodes triggered by minor events, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score of 23 meets the threshold for probable major depressive disorder with peripartum onset and co-occurring anxiety. You endorse loss of pleasure and humor, daily low mood, excessive guilt over routine infant care, intrusive worries, two recent panic-like attacks, and severe sleep disruption, all present most of the time. These symptoms map onto <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and align with heightened anxiety. Because scores ≥14 warrant urgent evaluation, immediate follow-up is recommended. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>PCP</med> or perinatal mental-health specialist
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or compatible antidepressant options
3. Plan daily 15-minute support windows-accept help with chores, meals, or night feeds to improve rest
4. Practice brief breathing or grounding exercises when panic sensations arise
5. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Screening Note – Postpartum Mood/Anxiety (EPDS items 1-10)

Symptoms/Concerns endorsed
- Anhedonia: marked loss of laughter, anticipatory enjoyment (items 1, 2)
- Persistent low mood, daily tearfulness, sense of “heavy cloud” (items 8, 9)
- Excessive guilt/self-blame re infant care (item 3)
- Daily, intrusive anxious worries (feeding, breathing, SIDS) with nocturnal checking (item 4)
- Two recent panic equivalents (sudden dyspnea, chest tightness, grounding needed) (item 5)
- Subjective overwhelm by routine tasks; “treading water” (item 6)
- Mood-related insomnia—rumination prevents initiation; fragmented 2-hour blocks (item 7)
- Denies any self-harm ideation; protective of infant (item 10)

Pattern
Consistent with moderate–severe depressive and comorbid anxiety symptoms emerging since delivery; functional impact on sleep, self-care, and infant-related confidence. No safety concerns to self or infant reported.

Screening significance
Elevated probability for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety disorder; recommend formal clinical interview (DSM-5-TR criteria) and standardized rating scales (EPDS, PHQ-9, GAD-7) to confirm severity and inform level-of-care decision.
